content: Good evening. I appreciate you making time tonight — I know I did not give you much lead time but I needed to talk through something before I lose another week to circular thinking. I have been sitting on a decision for about ten days now and every time I try to reason it out on my own I end up in a different place depending on what mood I am in. The issue is about a second location. Hamada — the broker from Plaza Homes that Daichi Sasaki introduced me to — reached out again yesterday afternoon. He has been patient with me, but I could tell from the tone of the call that he is feeling some urgency. He showed me a property in Tomigaya about ten days ago and has been waiting for a serious response. I told him I needed more time to think it through properly. The honest problem is that I do not even know what framework I should be using to evaluate something like this at this stage of the restaurant's life. We have only just passed the one-year mark, Petrelli has opinions about it, Hamada is pushing, and I keep going in circles. Can we work through it tonight? I want to walk out of this conversation with an actual position I can hold.

Of course, and I am glad you brought it here rather than letting it keep cycling. The dynamic you are describing — broker presenting an opportunity, restaurant doing well, external pressure building — is one that has a way of feeling more urgent than it actually is, partly because the person presenting the opportunity has a professional incentive to move quickly, and that urgency can distort the evaluation in ways that are hard to detect when you are inside the situation. Let us remove the urgency entirely and build the picture the right way. I want to understand several things before we form any view. First, what is the property itself — the specifics of location, size, rent, condition, and the fit-out situation you would be walking into. Second, where is Osteria Morishita right now in its own operational maturity and financial trajectory, because that context changes the risk calculation significantly. And third, what are the voices inside your own organization saying, particularly from the people who would be most directly affected by any expansion. You said Hamada showed you a property in Tomigaya. Let us start there and work outward. Walk me through exactly what he put in front of you.

Right. So Hamada brought me to see the space in person last week, which is partly why I have been thinking about it so intensively — seeing a physical room makes it real in a way that a listing does not. The property is in Tomigaya, which surprised me when Hamada first suggested it because Tomigaya is not a neighborhood I had thought about at all for a restaurant of this type. My instinct about Tomigaya has always been that it skews younger and more casual — great natural wine bars, inventive noodle spots, that kind of thing. Not the obvious home for a serious regional Italian operation with the kind of sourcing discipline and price point that we operate at. Hamada made a reasonably coherent case that the dining culture there has been shifting upward over the past couple of years, and he sent me some recent lease comps afterward that partially support that read. There are two or three more ambitious Western dining concepts that have taken root in the neighborhood recently, so he is not wrong that the mix has been changing. I do not fully discount his read — he is good at his job. But I also know it is his job to make the property sound attractive. The space itself: it is 18.2 tsubo. Not tiny but definitely not a big room. The previous tenant was in there for five years and vacated about four months ago. There is no usable fit-out — they stripped the space clean when they left, so we would be starting from nothing on the interior. And the rent is 580,000 yen per month. That is the headline number Hamada led with and it is the one I have been stress-testing ever since.

That is a useful and concrete set of facts to anchor on. Let me work through each element before we try to synthesize anything. On the neighborhood: Hamada is not wrong that Tomigaya has been moving. The area around Yoyogi Park and the streets running up toward Kamiyamacho have been attracting a more serious dining sensibility over the past year and a half, and there are operators who know what they are doing who have placed bets there without making a lot of noise about it. It is not where Azabu or Hiroo or Minami-Aoyama are in terms of established premium dining geography, but the mismatch is narrowing. The guest profile that frequents Tomigaya has the spending power and the appetite for serious food — the challenge is that they have to discover you before you can build any kind of loyalty. That is a different kind of opening period than one where you drop into a neighborhood that already has a trained population of diners looking for something like what you offer. On the 18.2 tsubo footprint: this is a number worth sitting with. At that size you are realistically looking at somewhere between eighteen and twenty-four seats depending on how you configure the room — whether you incorporate a bar counter, how much space you allocate per cover, what the kitchen takes up. For the style of dining that Osteria Morishita does, you would not want to push toward the top of that range. Something around twenty to twenty-two seats at a generous pitch is probably the right mental model, and that is a real constraint on your revenue capacity per service. On the rent: 580,000 yen per month is not outrageous for Tokyo, and for a neighborhood with the trajectory Hamada is describing it is not obviously overpriced. The question is not whether it is a fair number in the abstract — it is what that obligation requires of you operationally to be viable, and whether Osteria Morishita is in a position to absorb the ramp-up period that any new location demands. Have you started working through the math on what that rent level actually requires?

I have, and I did several rounds of it. The first was on the train home right after Hamada called yesterday, and the second was late last night when I could not sleep. If I run twenty-two seats at an average check comparable to Higashi-Azabu — let us say 22,000 yen per cover including drinks, which is roughly where we average on a normal dinner service — and I assume 75 percent capacity on dinner service six nights a week, I get to somewhere around 4.7 to 4.8 million yen monthly gross revenue in what I would call a reasonably good month. Rent at 580,000 yen is about 12 percent of that figure, which on the surface sounds manageable. I know operators who run well at 10 to 12 percent rent-to-revenue. So on paper, in the optimistic case, the math is not impossible. But every time I look at that number I keep coming back to the same problem: it requires 75 percent capacity, and 75 percent capacity is a fantasy for the first six months of a new location in a neighborhood where we have zero existing recognition and no existing customer base to draw from. Then I add staffing at the second location on top of what we are already running at Higashi-Azabu, the fit-out investment for a space that has been stripped clean, the amortization on that build-out, and the inescapable fact that my own attention would be split between two operations instead of concentrated on one. When I try to model what the numbers look like in the realistic scenario rather than the optimistic one, the picture changes considerably and that is where the unease starts.

Your instinct to push past the optimistic scenario is exactly right, and I want to be direct about what the numbers actually look like when you apply realistic ramp dynamics instead of steady-state assumptions. A new restaurant opening in a neighborhood where you are not known, with no transplantable loyal customer base and no existing brand presence in the local market, will typically run at somewhere between 30 and 50 percent of its target capacity through the first three months. If word-of-mouth builds well and you generate media attention, you might reach 55 to 65 percent by month five or six. Sustaining 75 percent on a regular basis would be a genuinely strong outcome at the twelve-month mark and is not something you can plan around at the outset. Apply those dynamics to your model: at 40 percent capacity with twenty-two seats, a 22,000 yen average check, and six dinner services a week, your monthly gross revenue is somewhere around 2.3 to 2.5 million yen. Suddenly 580,000 yen in rent is not 12 percent — it is closer to 23 to 25 percent of revenue, and you are paying that before food cost, labor, utilities, or any of the other fixed and variable costs that a restaurant carries. You would be looking at operating losses during the ramp-up period that could run well above a million yen per month in a realistic scenario, potentially for six to nine months. If the ramp takes longer — and it sometimes does in a neighborhood where you are establishing from zero — the cumulative cash exposure becomes significant. That is on top of the fit-out investment for a stripped space, which for a kitchen-forward concept like Osteria Morishita could be substantial. All of this is happening simultaneously with the Higashi-Azabu location, which does not stop needing your attention just because a second location opens. If anything it may need more of your presence during a period when you are least able to give it. Before we go further, I want to ask you directly: where is Osteria Morishita right now in its own lifecycle? Because the risk calculation for a second location looks completely different depending on whether you are operating from a position of consolidated, fully understood strength, or whether the first location still has gaps in your own knowledge of it.

That is exactly the question I keep running into in my own thinking, and I am glad you made it explicit because I do not think I have been asking it clearly enough. We opened in May of last year, so we are thirteen months in now. The one-year mark not reached yet in any meaningful operational sense when Hamada first brought this to me, and even now we have only barely cleared it. I do not feel like I have finished building the first business yet. Revenue has been solid and the critical reception has been genuinely better than I expected — the Tabelog rating is moving, we got a press mention in March that drove a real spike in reservations, the repeat customer rate has been building in a way that I find encouraging. All of those things are true. But I have not been through a full annual cycle in a way where I can say with confidence that I actually understand the business in all its seasons and moods. Last February was rough — occupancy dropped significantly and I could not give you a clean explanation for why. Was it seasonal demand, a service consistency problem that month, a staffing gap that showed up in the guest experience, some combination of all three? I genuinely do not know. I have never had a February to compare it against before. I have been learning this business through a single cycle and there are real gaps in my own knowledge of its operating characteristics, its vulnerabilities, its actual demand pattern across a full year. The idea of compounding that by taking on a second location before those gaps are closed — before I have actually finished understanding the first operation — keeps landing somewhere close to irresponsible. I keep pulling back from that word but I am not sure I should.

Do not pull back from it. Irresponsible is not too strong a word for what you are describing, and I want to encourage you to stay with it rather than softening it out of politeness to Hamada or to your own ambition. The instinct you are articulating is one of the most important things a restaurant operator can develop, and the fact that you are applying it to your own situation rather than letting the momentum of a growth opportunity override it reflects a clear-headedness that actually matters here. What you are describing is a documented and recurring failure pattern in restaurant expansion. A first location builds momentum. That momentum generates optimism. An opportunity appears. And the operator interprets the momentum as evidence of readiness to scale. But momentum and consolidation are genuinely different things. Momentum means the business is trending in a positive direction. Consolidation means you understand why it is trending that way with sufficient depth that you could protect it, replicate it, or correct a deviation from it. You just told me that you cannot explain what happened in February. That is not a crisis, but it is a real knowledge gap — and if you cannot explain February in the first location, you cannot build a reliable staffing model, cash buffer strategy, or operating forecast for either location with any confidence. The decision to open a second location is essentially a decision to multiply the complexity you are managing before you have fully mastered the first instance of it. That is not a risk that better lease terms or a more favorable neighborhood can offset — it is a structural timing problem. I want to bring another voice into this. You have mentioned Petrelli in several of our recent sessions and his view of the restaurant's direction has consistently been important to how you think. Has he weighed in on the Tomigaya opportunity specifically?

He has, and this is one of the more substantive inputs I have had through all of this. I sat down with Petrelli for a real conversation about it after I came back from seeing the Tomigaya space, before I called Hamada back. Petrelli is not someone who performs enthusiasm he does not feel, so I pay close attention to how he actually frames things rather than just what he says on the surface. He was not dismissive of the expansion idea at all — in fact I would say he was genuinely interested and in some ways energized. He has been wanting to build something with more reach for a while. He said he would be interested in expansion with Modena focus preserved. That was essentially his phrasing, and he was careful about it. He is deeply protective of what we have built culinarily — the sourcing relationships, the seasonal specificity, the way the menu carries a genuine regional identity rather than a generic Italian fine-dining template. His concern, which he stated plainly, was that running two kitchens simultaneously without adequate operational infrastructure in place would not carry the Modena focus forward to a second location. It would compromise it at both locations. He was specific about the sourcing dimension — the relationships with producers, the discipline around ingredients that are sometimes available in limited quantities, the seasonal decision-making that requires someone who understands both the product and the restaurant's culinary logic. Those things are not easy to divide or replicate. The condition he put on any expansion is, I think, a real and serious constraint on the timeline, even if I decided that the financial and operational timing were otherwise right. It is not a decorative preference. It is a load-bearing requirement for the identity of the restaurant.

Petrelli's framing deserves more weight than it might appear to carry at first reading, and I want to be precise about why. When your head chef tells you he would be interested in expansion with Modena focus preserved, he is not expressing an aesthetic preference that could be managed with better planning. He is identifying an operational dependency that is structural to what Osteria Morishita actually is. The culinary identity of the restaurant is not a brand that can be installed at a new location through a style guide and a training program. It is built on a very specific architecture: sourcing relationships with producers who supply ingredients with a particular provenance and quality standard; a seasonal menu cadence that requires someone with deep knowledge of what is available, when, in what quantity, and at what price; and the ability to communicate the story behind each dish credibly because the person communicating it is the person who built the relationships and made the decisions. All of that currently lives in Petrelli. It is embodied in him in a way that does not distribute easily across two parallel operations. To open a second location that genuinely carries the Modena focus would require one of two things. Either Petrelli divides his time and attention between the two kitchens, which means both operations receive a diminished version of his presence and the sourcing decisions, menu evolution, and kitchen culture at both locations suffer. Or you invest the time and energy to identify, hire, and develop a second chef who can carry the culinary identity without Petrelli's direct supervision — a project that realistically takes eighteen to twenty-four months to execute properly and that requires a period of intensive parallel management before you could trust the result. Neither path is fast. Neither is inexpensive in terms of time, money, or the trust Petrelli has placed in how this restaurant operates. When I bring together everything you have told me tonight — the math on the ramp-up period versus what 580,000 yen per month requires, the knowledge gaps in the first location that you have not yet had time to close, the structural condition Petrelli has set on any expansion — I am seeing a consistent signal. These are not isolated concerns pointing in different directions. They are all pointing toward the same conclusion. I want to ask you something directly. If you strip away the external pressure from Hamada and the social dimension of feeling like you should be at a stage where you field serious expansion opportunities — what does your own judgment tell you about the timing?

My judgment tells me it is too early. I think I have known that since the moment Hamada showed me the space. I just have not been willing to say it clearly because there is a lot of noise around the question that makes it feel more complicated than it actually is. Part of that noise is Hamada, who is genuinely skilled at what he does and who can make almost any opportunity sound more compelling than a cold-eyed analysis would support. Part of it is Daichi, who introduced us and who I know would be at least a little disappointed if I passed without seriously engaging with the idea. But the largest part of it is something I have to be honest about: ego. I am 34 years old. My friends from university who went into finance and consulting and technology are at stages in their careers where they are running teams, making decisions that scale, building things with multiple components. And there is a version of this story where opening a second restaurant is my version of that — evidence that the first one worked and now we multiply it. But that is not a business argument. That is a story I am unconsciously trying to write about my own life, and it is not a sound basis for a decision that would materially affect Petrelli's career, my team's stability, and the financial health of something I have spent more than a year building. When I actually strip away that noise and look at what is in front of me — the one-year mark not reached yet in any real sense of operational confidence, Petrelli's legitimate concern about culinary integrity under a split-attention scenario, the cash exposure during a Tomigaya ramp that could run for the better part of a year — I think the answer is clear. I just need to say it out loud and commit to it.

Then say it, and I will say it alongside you: the right decision is to pass on Tomigaya. And let me be clear about something important — passing is not a retreat from ambition. It is not the cautious option versus the bold option. Passing on this property at this moment, for these specific and well-reasoned grounds, is the more ambitious long-term move because it protects the thing you have already built while you complete the work of understanding it fully. What I want to do now is make sure this does not simply feel like deferring a decision into the fog. Deferral without structure has a way of leading to the same conversation happening again in five or six months when another opportunity appears, driven by the same external pressure and the same internal noise. What you need is a defined moment to revisit the question with actual criteria attached — a specific point in time where you can look at the business and honestly assess whether the conditions that are currently missing are now present. Your fiscal year ends in September 2026. That is a meaningful and natural inflection point. By then you will have been through every season of the business at least once. You will have data to explain what happened in February and whether it recurred. You will have a cleaner picture of whether the revenue trajectory reflects structural demand or is still variable in ways you do not yet fully understand. You will have had time to think about what Petrelli's condition actually requires in operational terms — what staffing, what infrastructure, what sourcing redundancy — before any second location could meet it credibly. My recommendation is to revisit second location after fiscal year end September 2026 — not as a vague aspiration but as a scheduled strategic review with defined criteria for readiness. That gives you four months to close the knowledge gaps, build the infrastructure, and arrive at the decision from a position of genuine strength rather than momentum. In the meantime, I want to raise something. If the instinct to grow is real — and it clearly is, and it is a healthy instinct — there is a direction that captures some of that energy without requiring a new lease, a new fit-out, a parallel management structure, or Petrelli dividing himself between two kitchens. I have been thinking about something you mentioned in passing a few weeks ago. Tell me about the back section of the dining room.

I had a feeling you were going to go there. The back section has been in the back of my mind for a while but the second-location conversation has been consuming the growth bandwidth in my head and I have not given it the serious attention it probably deserves. So: we have a portion of the dining room at Higashi-Azabu that seats eight people. It is technically part of the main floor but the layout of the space means it already functions semi-separately from the rest of the room. The sightlines are different, the ambient noise from the main floor does not reach it at the same level, and there is a natural transition point in the floor plan between that section and the rest of the dining room. I have had at least four or five separate inquiries from guests over the past six months asking whether we offer private dining. Each time I have had to tell them we do not currently offer it. One of those inquiries was a corporate group that wanted to reserve the entire back section for a client dinner — that would have been a meaningful event and I had to turn it away. Petrelli, interestingly, has mentioned the private dining room conversion himself. He brought it up a few months ago unprompted. His view is that the bones of the space already lend themselves to it — we would need to add a proper door to separate it acoustically from the main room, do some targeted lighting work to give it a more intimate character, and reconfigure the service path slightly so that the team can reach that section without moving through the main dining room in a way that disrupts both groups. The fit-out investment would be real but it is scoped and contained. It is not a full restaurant build-out from nothing. It is targeted improvements to a section we already occupy under an existing lease. And the economics are interesting. A buy-out of that section at a fixed minimum spend per event would be a different and more predictable revenue profile than cover-by-cover dinner service. Private dining clients also tend to be significantly less price-sensitive than walk-in or reservation covers. I think I want to move forward on that — launch a private dining room conversion in the existing space and put the second-location question on hold until after September. Does that feel like the right call?

It is not just the right call — it is the stronger strategic move for where Osteria Morishita is right now, and I want to explain why it is genuinely stronger rather than simply safer, because when you tell Hamada you are passing and when Daichi hears about it, there will be a natural tendency for people who care about your success to frame the private dining room as a consolation prize compared to expansion. It is not. Let me be specific about what a private dining room conversion in the existing Higashi-Azabu space actually accomplishes. First, it deepens the premium positioning of the restaurant rather than diluting it by spreading the identity across two addresses. A launch of private dining room service at a fixed minimum spend — and you should be thinking about a minimum in a range that reflects the caliber of the experience you are offering — communicates exclusivity. That signal raises the perceived standing of the main room as well. Guests who know you offer private experiences for serious groups will form a different impression of what they are participating in when they sit in the main dining room. It reinforces the identity upward rather than spreading it sideways. Second, the cash flow profile of private dining buy-outs is categorically different from table-by-table cover service. A confirmed event with a deposit is revenue you can see and plan around. It is not subject to the same weather variability, last-minute cancellations, or slow-Tuesday unpredictability that regular dinner service carries. As you build a base of corporate clients and repeat special-occasion groups, those relationships compound in a way that individual reservations do not. Third, and this matters enormously given what Petrelli said: the culinary operation stays in one kitchen, one team, one location. There is no division of his attention. There is no sourcing pipeline that gets split between two addresses. The condition he articulated — interested in expansion with Modena focus preserved — is fully honored by a private dining room that operates as an intensified expression of what Higashi-Azabu already does, not a parallel operation that competes with it. Fourth, the investment is scoped and contained. You are not absorbing 580,000 yen per month in new rent obligations on top of your current base. You are investing in targeted fit-out improvements within a space you already lease, and those improvements will be amortized against the revenue the room generates. The execution risk is orders of magnitude lower than a new location. Let us spend the rest of this session mapping out what the private dining room conversion would actually require. That means sequencing the physical work, arriving at a realistic investment estimate, thinking about how to position and price it publicly, what the minimum spend structure should look like for different event formats, and how you communicate to Hamada that you value the relationship and are not closing the door on future opportunities — just not this property, not now.
